lessons.key_idea: At West Point, a simple grit score predicted which cadets would survive brutal summer training better than their talent-based admission scores did.

lessons.title: Effort Counts Twice
lessons.key_idea: Effort turns talent into skill and then turns skill into achievement, so it matters twice as much as talent alone.

lessons.title: Passion Is Developed, Not Found
lessons.key_idea: Lasting interest rarely arrives as a sudden spark; it grows slowly through exploration, then deepens as we keep discovering new things in the same field.

lessons.title: Practice That Actually Makes You Better
lessons.key_idea: Experts improve through deliberate practice: targeting a specific weakness, working on it with full focus, getting feedback, and repeating.

lessons.title: Finding a Purpose Beyond Yourself
lessons.key_idea: Grit grows stronger when we see our work as connected to the well-being of others, the way one bricklayer sees himself building a cathedral rather than just laying bricks.

lessons.title: Hope Keeps You Getting Back Up
lessons.key_idea: Gritty people expect their own efforts can improve their future, so they treat setbacks as temporary and fixable rather than proof they lack ability.

lessons.title: Growing Grit From the Outside In
lessons.key_idea: Parents, activities and cultures build grit by being both demanding and supportive, such as a family Hard Thing Rule where everyone sticks with a challenging pursuit.

plan.title: Grit
plan.author: Angela Duckworth
plan.confidence_note: I know this book's core arguments, structure, and main examples well, including the West Point research, the effort equations, and the four psychological assets of grit.
plan.one_liner: Why sticking with a long-term goal beats raw talent, and how anyone can grow that staying power.
plan.summary: Psychologist Angela Duckworth asks why some people achieve so much more than others with similar ability. Her answer is grit, a blend of passion and perseverance for a long-term goal. Drawing on her research with West Point cadets, spelling bee finalists, salespeople and students, she shows that grit often predicts success better than talent or test scores. She argues that talent matters, but effort counts twice: once in building skill and again in turning skill into achievement. Gritty people tend to share four traits. They have a deep interest, they practice deliberately, they feel a sense of purpose, and they hold on to hope after setbacks. Duckworth's encouraging message is that grit is not fixed. It can be grown from the inside, and also from the outside through supportive parents, challenging activities and cultures that value persistence.
